area: Foundation crates: celnet-types, celnet-core, celnet-conventions, celnet-calendar

findings.issue: VanillaInputs::df_dom/df_for/forward compute discount factors and the outright forward via a helper named `libm_exp` that actually calls the std intrinsic `x.exp()`, NOT `libm`. The comment (lines 325-328) explicitly justifies using `f64::exp` 'to keep this crate leaf-pure'. These values feed celnet-vanilla::price (lib.rs:67-68 uses i.df_for()/i.df_dom()) and the strike<->delta solver (solver.rs:72 uses template.forward()), i.e. the actual pricing path.
findings.why_it_matters: CLAUDE.md guardrail #5 and the determinism rule require all transcendentals to route through libm via celnet-core::math so results are bit-identical across OS/arch. The system libm `exp` differs in the last ULP between platforms; that difference propagates into df, forward, price and every Greek, breaking reproducible/auditable pricing and any cross-platform golden-file or GPU-vs-CPU reconciliation. The helper name `libm_exp` is also actively misleading: it lies about its own implementation.
findings.recommended_fix: Route the derived-quantity exp through libm. Either add a `libm` dependency to celnet-types (it is a tiny leaf crate, libm has no deps) and call `libm::exp`, or move df/forward derivation out of celnet-types into celnet-core::math (which already wraps libm::exp) and have the engine compute them. Delete the false 'libm_exp' name/comment.

findings.issue: canonicalize() resolves a flipped pair to the covered profile (CADUSD -> USDCAD profile) and returns that profile's record verbatim, including premium_style and the premium-adjusted/forward delta. The profile is written for the market-quoted orientation (USDCAD: premium in USD = base/FOR -> premium-adjusted). When the caller queries the inverted orientation CADUSD (base=CAD, quote=USD), the returned record still says premium_style=PercentForeign and delta=SpotPremiumAdjusted, but in the CADUSD orientation 'foreign/base' is now CAD, so the premium-in-USD is actually in the QUOTE currency and the delta should be premium-UNADJUSTED. The test flipped_legs_resolve_to_same_profile (registry.rs:388-395) asserts the records are identical, baking in the bug.
findings.why_it_matters: ConventionRecord.premium_style and is_delta_premium_adjusted drive the strike<->delta inversion and the hedge delta downstream (record.rs:79-108). A wrong premium-adjustment flag for the inverted orientation systematically corrupts every strike, smile node and hedge for that pair when quoted the 'wrong' way round - exactly the 'convention error dwarfs model error' failure the crate exists to prevent. FX systems do quote inverted majors in practice.
findings.recommended_fix: Either (a) restrict canonicalize to only accept the canonical orientation and return None for the inverted one (forcing region default, which is orientation-correct), or (b) when a flip is detected, transform the record to the caller's orientation: swap which leg is FOR/DOM, recompute premium_style/premium-adjusted relative to the queried base, and swap the accrual day-counts. Update the test to assert orientation-correct (not identical) records.

findings.issue: The US settlement centre is documented as 'US Federal Reserve / SIFMA bond-market days' but encodes Columbus Day (2nd Mon Oct) and Veterans Day (11 Nov) as closures. For FX settlement the relevant calendar is Fedwire/USD bank settlement (and de-facto NYSE for the spot/option market), which is NOT closed on Columbus Day or Veterans Day - those are SIFMA bond-market recommended closes only. Conversely the doc/code conflate two different calendars (Fed vs SIFMA) under one centre.
findings.why_it_matters: Treating Columbus Day and Veterans Day as USD non-business days shifts spot, expiry and delivery dates for every USD-legged and cross-via-USD pair around those dates, and pulls them into vol-time year fractions. That is a real, recurring date error twice a year on most of the G10 book - a settlement/PV bug, not cosmetic.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the calendar's purpose (FX settlement = Fedwire/NYSE). For FX, drop Columbus Day and Veterans Day from the USD settlement set (Fedwire is open; spot still settles). If a SIFMA bond calendar is genuinely needed elsewhere, model it as a separate CentreId rather than overloading the FX USD centre. Align the doc comment with whichever calendar is chosen and cite the source.

findings.issue: Japanese substitute-holiday handling is incomplete. (1) The transfer-holiday (furikae kyujitsu) rule only checks the immediately preceding day (lines 346-352), so it cannot handle the case where a holiday's substitute itself lands on another holiday (Golden Week / consecutive holidays) - the substitute must roll to the next non-holiday weekday, not just Monday. (2) The 'citizens holiday' (kokumin no kyujitsu) rule is acknowledged as not implemented (lines 353-355) - it is hard-coded as 'covered by Greenery Day', which is only true post-2007; it also arises in other sandwich configurations (e.g. when Respect-for-the-Aged Monday and the Autumnal Equinox are separated by one weekday in some years). (3) Marine Day/Sports Day one-off moves for the 2020/2021 Olympics are not handled.
findings.why_it_matters: JPY is one of the two cut regions (Tokyo 1500) and USDJPY is a worked example throughout the spec. Missed/miscomputed Tokyo closures shift USDJPY and all JPY-cross spot/expiry/delivery dates and vol-time, producing wrong T and wrong settlement on a core pair. The crate explicitly claims 'real public holidays, not placeholders'.
findings.recommended_fix: Implement furikae as 'roll the observed date forward to the next day that is neither a Sunday nor a public holiday' (loop, not single-step), implement the kokumin-no-kyujitsu sandwich rule generally (any weekday flanked by two holidays becomes a holiday), and either encode the 2020/2021 Olympic one-offs or document the supported year range explicitly. Add reference-date tests for a Golden Week with a Sunday-anchored holiday.

findings.issue: Tenor::Weeks(w) is converted to months via integer `w / 5`, an ad-hoc heuristic (5 weeks = 1 month). This makes 4W -> 0 months and, more importantly, large week tenors mis-classify the spot/forward delta axis: Tenor::Weeks(60) (~13.8 months, genuinely > 1Y) computes 60/5 = 12 months and is therefore treated as 'short' (spot delta) instead of long (forward delta). Same family: Tenor::Months(13..) is handled correctly but week-expressed long tenors are not.
findings.why_it_matters: The headline term-structure rule (spot delta short, forward delta long, the USDJPY worked example) can be silently wrong for week-expressed long tenors, returning the wrong DeltaConvention. Week tenors beyond a few weeks are unusual but the registry accepts them and the mapping is not defensible.
findings.recommended_fix: Convert weeks to an approximate day/month count consistent with the spot/forward boundary using days (e.g. weeks*7 > 365 -> long), or reject week tenors above a small bound. Add a test for a long week tenor.

findings.issue: is_close uses a symmetric max-magnitude relative tolerance and an exact `a == b` fast path. Two concerns: (1) the audit rule 'all float compare via is_close/assert_close, never ==' is technically violated by the internal `a == b` on line 20 - it is guarded and arguably the intended canonical equality, but it should be called out as the single sanctioned exception (it also means is_close(0.0, -0.0) returns true, which is fine but undocumented). (2) The relative branch `diff <= rel * a.abs().max(b.abs())` will report values of opposite sign with small magnitudes as close via the abs() branch only, which is correct, but there is no guard that rel/abs are non-negative/finite, so a caller passing a NaN tolerance silently makes everything 'not close'.
findings.why_it_matters: Tolerance discipline is the backbone of every numerical assertion in the platform; the one `==` is fine but should be explicitly documented as the sole exception so future reviewers do not flag or 'fix' it, and so the rule's intent is unambiguous. NaN tolerances would silently weaken every assertion that derived a tolerance from a computed quantity.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a doc line marking line 20 as the single sanctioned exact-equality use (covers exact-equal and +/-0). Optionally debug_assert!(rel.is_finite() && rel >= 0.0 && abs.is_finite() && abs >= 0.0) to catch malformed tolerances in tests.

findings.issue: as_str() uses `core::str::from_utf8(&self.0).unwrap_or("???")`. The bytes are validated ASCII-alphabetic on every constructor (new/parse) and the only field is private, so from_utf8 cannot fail; the `unwrap_or("???")` is dead defensive code that can mask a future invariant break by silently returning a sentinel currency code instead of failing loudly.
findings.why_it_matters: A silent '???' would propagate as a bogus currency through Display, pair keys (registry::key indexes bytes b[0..3]) and logs rather than surfacing the bug; for a frozen base type, masking corruption is worse than panicking in debug. Minor because the invariant currently holds.
findings.recommended_fix: Use `from_utf8(&self.0).expect("Ccy bytes are validated ASCII on construction")`, or store as a validated newtype that makes the conversion infallible by construction. Remove the '???' sentinel.

findings.issue: The Japanese equinox holidays are computed with a floating-point polynomial approximation valid only for 1980-2099 (documented), using f64 multiply + floor inside otherwise-exact civil-date logic. Outside that window the day is wrong, and the function silently returns a value rather than signalling the unsupported year. The whole crate's lib.rs claims 'no floating point in the calendar logic itself' (line 28), which this contradicts.
findings.why_it_matters: For long-dated FX options (the crate supports Years(n) tenors and the spec emphasizes >1Y term structure), expiries can fall beyond 2099, where the equinox day silently desynchronises Tokyo closures, shifting JPY dates and vol-time. The 'no floating point in calendar logic' claim is stale/overstated given this f64 path. Minor today, but it is an undocumented correctness cliff and a docs-vs-code mismatch.
findings.recommended_fix: Either compute the equinox from an integer table per decade, or assert/clamp the supported year range and document it on the public schedule/expiry functions. Correct the lib.rs determinism claim to 'integer date arithmetic except the bounded equinox approximation and the daycount division'.

findings.issue: AUDUSD/NZDUSD profiles hard-code day_count_accrual_for = Act365Fixed for AUD/NZD, while the region_default path (accrual_basis, lines 113-119) only special-cases GBP and assigns Act360 to everything else including AUD/NZD. So a covered AUDUSD gets ACT/365 for the AUD leg but an uncovered AUD-legged cross (e.g. AUDJPY) gets ACT/360 for the AUD leg from the region default - an internal inconsistency in the same currency's accrual basis depending only on whether the pair is in the covered set.
findings.why_it_matters: Accrual day-count should be a property of the currency, not of whether the pair happens to have a bespoke profile. The inconsistency yields different money-market discounting for the same currency across pairs, a subtle PV/forward error and a maintainability trap.
findings.recommended_fix: Make accrual_basis the single source of truth per currency (add AUD, NZD as Act365Fixed there) and have both PairProfile::record_at and region_default derive accrual day-counts from it, rather than hard-coding per profile.

findings.issue: DayCount supports only Act365Fixed and Act360. State-of-the-art FX/rates day-counts used in real curve building and accrual include ACT/ACT (ISDA), 30/360, and Business/252 (BRL). The lib.rs §coverage and the conventions registry assume only the two bases. There is no NDF fixing-date / fixing-calendar concept either: Settlement::NonDeliverable exists, but the calendar/schedule layer has no fixing date (typically expiry - N business days on the reference fixing calendar, distinct from delivery), so an NDF's economically critical fixing date is not modelled.
findings.why_it_matters: Competition (Fenics/Bloomberg/Murex-class) models full day-count families and, crucially for EM, the NDF fixing schedule (fixing date, fixing source, settlement currency). The audit lane explicitly calls out 'NDF' coverage: the registry flags settlement=NonDeliverable but the date engine produces only spot/expiry/delivery, never a fixing date, so NDF pricing/settlement is incomplete vs state-of-the-art.
findings.recommended_fix: Extend DayCount with ActAct (ISDA) and Bus252 as needed for covered currencies, and add a fixing-date computation (and fixing calendar / settlement-currency field) to FxSchedule / ConventionRecord for non-deliverable pairs so the NDF chain is horizon->spot->fixing->settlement, not just delivery.

findings.issue: Spot-lag exceptions are limited to a hard-coded T+1 USD set (CAD/TRY/RUB/PHP) and there is no handling of the USD-holiday spot-lag subtlety: for non-USD pairs the market convention is that the USD calendar is used to *count* spot lag but a USD holiday between trade and spot does not extend the lag for pairs not involving USD (it only blocks the value date). Here calendar_for adds USD to every cross and add_business_days requires USD open for every intermediate day, which over-extends spot for crosses around US holidays. Also there is no T+1 for same-currency-zone majors beyond the USD list, and no T+0 (e.g. USDCAD intraday) or T+2-with-USD-holiday-rule nuance.
findings.why_it_matters: Real FX spot conventions distinguish 'currency pair business days' from 'USD clearing days': a US holiday should not push a EURJPY spot date the way a TARGET2 or Tokyo holiday does, under the standard CLS/market rule. Over-extending spot dates shifts vol-time T and settlement for crosses around frequent US holidays - a systematic date error vs how Bloomberg/Reuters compute spot.
findings.recommended_fix: Implement the standard rule: compute spot lag on the two legs' joint calendar, then require the value date itself (not the intermediate count) to also be a USD good day for USD-cleared pairs; do not let a USD holiday in the lag window extend a non-USD cross's spot. Add reference tests against known EURJPY spot dates around 4 July.

findings.issue: Cut enumerates only NewYork1000 and Tokyo1500; real FX options also quote London, Frankfurt/ECB, and Sydney cuts, and the cut interacts with expiry time-of-day and vol-time (intraday). Tenor enumerates ON/Weeks/Months/Years but omits standard market tenors that are not simple multiples: Tom-Next/Spot-Next, and broken/IMM dates; there is also no way to express a fixed expiry Date directly (only relative tenors), which every real options system needs for bespoke deals.
findings.why_it_matters: Audit lane asks for cut completeness. Limiting cuts to two and tenors to relative-only means the vocabulary cannot represent a large fraction of the live market (e.g. an ECB-cut EUR option, a broken-dated trade, or a client-specified expiry date), capping completeness vs Synoption/Fenics. As a frozen base crate this is a hard ceiling on everything downstream.
findings.recommended_fix: Add London/Frankfurt/Sydney cuts (with their fixing times), add a fixed-Date expiry variant (or a separate ExpirySpec) alongside relative Tenor, and add Tom-Next/Spot-Next and broken-date support. Coordinate as a frozen-interface change per the parallel-session model.

findings.issue: norm_cdf is implemented correctly via 0.5*erfc(-x/sqrt2) (tail-stable, good). However the only tail test asserts norm_cdf(-40.0) >= 0.0 and norm_cdf(40.0) <= 1.0 - these are trivially true even for a broken implementation. There is no assertion that deep-tail values are *accurate* (e.g. norm_cdf(-37) ~ matching a reference, or that 1 - norm_cdf(x) == norm_cdf(-x) to high precision in the tail), and no test that the result never underflows to exactly 0.0 where a positive value is expected for moderately deep tails used in deep-OTM digital/barrier pricing.
findings.why_it_matters: Deep-tail accuracy of the normal CDF is load-bearing for far-OTM vanillas, digitals and barrier touch probabilities. A weak test (>= 0.0) would not catch a regression that, say, lost the erfc routing and reintroduced catastrophic cancellation. The implementation is right; the validation is not strong enough to protect it per guardrail #5 ('validated against references, never merely asserted plausible').
findings.recommended_fix: Add reference-valued tail assertions via assert_close against known Phi values (e.g. Phi(-1), Phi(-5), Phi(-10) from a published table/QuantLib) and a symmetry test norm_cdf(-x) close to 1 - norm_cdf(x) at x in {5,10,20} with tight tolerance.

overall: The four foundation crates are well-structured, documented, vendor-neutral in naming, and free of todo!/mocks/schema_version. Convention enums cover the 4 delta conventions, ATM (ATMF/DNS), premium styles, cut, day-count and NDF settlement, and the registry/calendar logic is mostly sound with good property tests. However there is one determinism BLOCKER: VanillaInputs::df/forward use the std `f64::exp` intrinsic (deceptively named `libm_exp`) instead of libm, and these feed the actual pricing path - directly violating the bit-identical-across-platforms guardrail. Two further MAJOR correctness issues: (a) inverted-orientation pairs (e.g. CADUSD) inherit the canonical profile's premium/delta labelling unchanged, mislabeling premium-adjustment for the queried orientation; (b) the US 'settlement' calendar includes SIFMA-only Columbus/Veterans Day closures that are not FX/Fedwire settlement holidays, shifting dates twice a year on most of the book; plus incomplete Japanese substitute/citizens-holiday logic on a core cut region. The remaining findings are accrual-basis inconsistency, week-to-month tenor mis-classification of long tenors, a stale 'no floating point' calendar claim (equinox uses f64, valid only 1980-2099), weak deep-tail norm_cdf validation, and state-of-the-art gaps (limited DayCount family, no NDF fixing date, only two cuts, no fixed-date/broken-date tenors, and an over-broad USD-holiday spot-lag rule for crosses). Fix the libm determinism violation and the orientation/US-calendar correctness bugs before treating these crates as frozen.

area: celnet-vanilla (GK price + 14 Greeks + delta conventions + strike-to-delta solver + ATM/DNS) and celnet-surface (Vanna-Volga, SABR, SVI/SSVI, broker-to-smile calibration, arbitrage gates, term structure)

findings.issue: The broker→smile strangle calibration solves the wrong equation. The standard Reiswich-Wystup/Clark market-strangle constraint is: build the smile from {ATM, smile-call-wing, smile-put-wing}, then evaluate that smile at the BROKER-strangle strikes (K_call^MS, K_put^MS) and require the two options priced at the SMILE's vols at those broker strikes to reproduce the market-strangle price. The implemented `residual` instead prices the *smile* wing strikes (call_strike/put_strike, themselves solved at the smile wing vols) at the smile wing vols and compares that sum to the broker-strangle sum. It never builds a VV smile inside the loop and never evaluates any smile at the broker strikes. The enforced identity V(K_smile_call,σ_smile_call)+V(K_smile_put,σ_smile_put) = V(K_broker_call,σ_strangle)+V(K_broker_put,σ_strangle) is a different, non-standard constraint that does not pin smile convexity to the broker strangle in the canonical way.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the exact failure the spec calls the '#1 production bug' (docs/ANALYTICS-SPEC.md §1.4): mis-recovering smile convexity from the broker butterfly silently biases the wings and breaks 10Δ reproduction. The calibrated σ_ss will generally differ from the true RW value, so the surface mismarks options between/beyond the 25Δ wings for high-RR/EM pairs — exactly where the distinction is material.
findings.recommended_fix: Inside `residual`, for each trial σ_ss build the VannaVolgaSmile from [put_wing, ATM, call_wing], evaluate it at the broker strikes ms.call_strike/ms.put_strike, price the two options at smile.implied_vol(broker_strike), and drive that sum to ms.price. Add a test asserting build_smile reprices ms.price at the broker strikes.

findings.issue: The 'reprices the broker quotes exactly' tests are near-vacuous. Every reprice assertion evaluates the VV smile at cal.call_strike/cal.put_strike (the smile wing strikes, which are exact benchmark pillars of the VV smile by construction) or re-sums vanillas at the smile wing (strike,vol) pairs. No test evaluates the constructed smile at the broker-strangle strikes ms.call_strike/ms.put_strike. grep confirms ms.call_strike/ms.put_strike are only used by the 'naive' comparison, never fed through smile.implied_vol().
findings.why_it_matters: The headline guarantee ('reprices the broker quotes exactly') is asserted by tests that cannot fail regardless of whether the calibration is correct, because they query the smile at its own benchmark pillars. The real RW constraint is untested, masking the strangle.rs calibration defect above.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a test: smile=build_smile(ctx,q); ms=market_strangle(...); assert is_close(price(Call,template(ms.call_strike, smile.implied_vol(ms.call_strike))) + price(Put,template(ms.put_strike, smile.implied_vol(ms.put_strike))), ms.price). It will currently fail and pin the fix.

findings.issue: The large-strike wing bound is coded as b·(1+|ρ|) ≤ 4/t and documented as 'the classic necessary large-strike bound (Gatheral 2004)'. In raw SVI, w(k) is TOTAL implied variance whose asymptotic slope is b(1+|ρ|); the Lee/Gatheral moment bound on that slope is dimensionless (≤ 2, or 4 under a specific normalization) and carries NO 1/t factor. Dividing by t makes the threshold maturity-dependent in a way the literature does not, so the check is too tight for short maturities and too loose for long ones.
findings.why_it_matters: A 'necessary no-arbitrage' diagnostic with the wrong threshold passes arbitrageable long-dated slices and rejects valid short-dated ones. It is exposed publicly and documented as a known no-arb condition, so consumers and the surface layer may trust it.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace 4.0/self.t with the dimensionless constant (b·(1+|ρ|) ≤ 2 for the total-variance slope, or 4 if matching a specific normalization) and remove the 1/t; cite the exact equation. Add a long-dated test where the bound and the density-factor scan agree.

findings.issue: The 'arbitrage-free SABR wing' is a single-step normal heuristic: it maps y(K) through the SABR x(z) function, places a Gaussian of std √t in the u-coordinate with du/dy=1/root, and is deliberately NOT normalised (the test only checks total mass within ±5e-2 of 1). density_implied_vol integrates this unnormalised density to reprice the wing call and re-implies a Black vol, inheriting the few-percent mass error. This is neither the Hagan-2014 arbitrage-free PDE nor the Antonov mapping; it is an approximation with systematic wing bias.
findings.why_it_matters: Wing vols outside the core band can be biased by the density's few-percent mass error, so the 'arbitrage-free' wing the surface falls back to is itself mispriced and not mass-consistent — below the state-of-the-art/competitor bar. It also makes the wing crossover (find_density_floor, strict <0 on an approximate density) noisy.
findings.recommended_fix: Implement the true Hagan-2014 arbitrage-free density PDE (or Antonov's exact mapping) so the density integrates to 1 and prices are consistent, or renormalise the integrated mass before re-implying the wing vol, tighten the normalisation test, and state the residual error budget.

findings.issue: Because the smile is never closed through the calibration loop, the smile-delta fixed point Δ_smile(K)=±dΔ at the smile vol is enforced only for the wing pillars, not jointly with the broker reprice. For strongly skewed smiles the joint (strike, vol, smile) fixed point and the broker reprice are not solved simultaneously.
findings.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the calibration is a decoupled approximation; 10Δ reproduction (the stated downstream check) is not guaranteed for skewed/EM smiles.
findings.recommended_fix: Fold smile construction into the residual (see first finding) so the strike/vol/smile fixed point and the broker reprice are solved jointly.

findings.issue: powf is exp(y·ln x). This is deterministic (libm exp/ln) so it satisfies the determinism rule, but is materially less accurate than a correctly-rounded pow for the CEV factor (F·K)^((1-β)/2) and the log-moneyness↔strike (e^k) maps, adding ~1-2 ulp error that propagates into SABR/SVI vols and the arbitrage second differences.
findings.why_it_matters: Wing-density second differences (arbitrage.rs, sabr.rs) are sensitive to small price errors; the extra rounding can shift the detected wing crossover and the min-density near the is_arbitrage_free tolerance boundary.
findings.recommended_fix: Use libm::pow (still rust-lang/libm, still bit-deterministic) exposed via celnet-core::math instead of exp∘ln, preserving the single-source-of-determinism invariant without precision loss.

findings.issue: Total-variance interpolation is linear in business time at fixed log-moneyness k, but the calendar guarantee is fixed-STRIKE (acknowledged in the module docstring). When pillar forwards differ, interior interpolation mixes pillar w(k) at the same k (different strikes), so monotone-in-k does not imply monotone-in-K. min_calendar_increment correctly re-evaluates at fixed strike, but the interpolation itself is not, and surface.rs samples only 3 k-levels (±span, 0).
findings.why_it_matters: For pairs with steep forward curves the interpolated mid-maturity surface can carry small calendar arbitrage between pillars that the 3-point increment scan misses, undermining the 'no calendar arbitrage by construction' claim in surface.rs docs.
findings.recommended_fix: Interpolate total variance at fixed strike (convert the query strike to each pillar's own k before interpolating), or densify the calendar-increment scan across many k and tie the 'arbitrage-free by construction' claim to the actual interpolation.

findings.issue: The function computes φ(d1) only to discard it (`let _ = norm_pdf(d1);`) and returns −Φ(d2), explicitly ignoring the ∂σ/∂K smile term in the strike slope (doc admits it is the 'sticky' slope). It is therefore not the true ∂c/∂K of the smile-consistent call and is not used by check_slice (which uses coarse finite differences instead).
findings.why_it_matters: A public 'slope-bound diagnostic' that omits the smile term can report a slope in [−1,0] for a slice that actually violates the vertical bound once the smile term is included; callers relying on it for digital-call probability validity get a flat-vol answer.
findings.recommended_fix: Either compute the full ∂c/∂K including φ(d1)·√t·(∂σ/∂K), or rename/document it as the explicitly-flat-vol slope and remove the dead norm_pdf call.

findings.issue: For unadjusted-delta, reachability for targets near the achievable extreme (spot-unadjusted max call delta is e^{-r_f T} < 1) is detected only by 64-iteration bracket-expansion exhaustion, not an explicit cap, so near-cap targets surface as Unreachable indirectly. Also delta_set_strikes_straddle_forward asserts kc>f for ALL four conventions including premium-adjusted, where the premium-adjusted 25Δ call strike is not guaranteed above the forward in general (holds for the chosen base only).
findings.why_it_matters: Edge targets near the spot-unadjusted cap are handled by iteration-budget exhaustion rather than a clean closed-form reachability test, so the Unreachable vs NoConvergence taxonomy can be inconsistent; the straddle geometry assertion may be over-broad.
findings.recommended_fix: Add explicit reachability caps (|target| ≤ e^{-r_f T} spot-unadjusted, ≤ 1 forward-unadjusted) before bracketing, returning Unreachable deterministically; relax the straddle test's kc>f claim for premium-adjusted to a convention-aware expectation.

findings.issue: Pillars are calibrated independently per delta; there is no joint 5-point (ATM+25Δ+10Δ) smile calibration that simultaneously reprices both broker strangles and both risk-reversals through one smile. build_smile uses only the 25Δ wings for the VV pillars and treats 10Δ as a 'validation' that is never asserted to reprice its own broker strangle.
findings.why_it_matters: Competitor FX smile engines (the stated bar) calibrate a single smile reproducing ATM, RR25, BF25, RR10, BF10 jointly; the decoupled per-pillar approach cannot guarantee the 10Δ broker strangle reprices once the 25Δ smile is fixed — the 10-delta-reproduction failure the spec warns about.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a joint multi-pillar calibration (SVI/SSVI or 5-point VV) that reprices all quoted broker strangles and risk-reversals through one smile, and assert 10Δ broker-strangle reproduction in tests.

findings.issue: SVI/SSVI provide evaluation and arbitrage diagnostics but NO calibration from market quotes/data. There is no fit of (a,b,ρ,m,σ) or (ρ,η,γ,θ_t) to broker quotes or to a market smile; slices are only constructed from hand-supplied parameters in tests. The surface layer cannot produce an SVI/SSVI surface from market input.
findings.why_it_matters: The crate's stated role (broker quotes → arbitrage-free surface, with SSVI 'the preferred globally-arbitrage-free production surface') is unmet for SVI/SSVI: without calibration these models cannot mark a market, so the arbitrage-free fallback the VV layer hands off to does not exist end-to-end.
findings.recommended_fix: Implement quasi-explicit SVI slice calibration (e.g. the quasi-explicit De Marco-Martini method) and an SSVI θ_t + (ρ,η,γ) fit to the calibrated pillars with arbitrage-constrained optimisation, plus tests that the calibrated SVI/SSVI reprice the broker quotes.

overall: The vanilla pricing core is strong and trustworthy: the Garman-Kohlhagen price, all 14 Greeks (including charm/color, whose dd1_dT closed form I verified by hand), put-call parity, the four delta conventions, the non-monotone premium-adjusted-call guard (closed-form K_max + decreasing-branch bracketing), and the DNS/ATMF sign rules are correct and validated against a 3200-row QuantLib golden grid plus finite-difference and property tests. No determinism violations in lane (no float ==/!= used as correctness comparisons; transcendentals route through celnet-core::math/libm; the only == are benign branch/guards). The Vanna-Volga second-approximation interpolation (weights p/q, D1, D2) matches Castagna-Mercurio and reprices its pillars exactly; the arbitrage detector genuinely fires on negative density (verified by the V-shaped test). The serious problems are in celnet-surface's market-data-facing layers: (1) the broker→smile strangle calibration solves a non-standard equation that never closes the VV smile through the broker strikes, and (2) the tests claiming 'reprices the broker quotes exactly' only query the smile at its own benchmark pillars, so they cannot detect that defect — together undermining the headline FX-smile guarantee (the spec's '#1 production bug'). Secondary issues: the SVI wing bound carries a spurious 1/t, the 'arbitrage-free' SABR wing is an unnormalised single-step heuristic (few-percent mass error), term-structure interpolation is fixed-k not fixed-strike (calendar guarantee weaker than claimed), and SVI/SSVI ship without calibration from market data, so the production arbitrage-free surface cannot be built end-to-end. Fix the calibration equation and its test first (correctness of the marked surface), then the SVI wing bound and the SABR wing density.

area: celnet-exotics: digitals, touches/DNT, single+double barriers, Vanna-Volga overlay, CN+Rannacher PDE, Philox/BB/BGK/CV Monte-Carlo, and the LSV (QE variance + Dupire/particle leverage + HV-ADI) booking model

findings.issue: In/out parity is enforced by construction (KO is computed as `vanilla - knock_in`, line 252), so the headline `in_out_parity_all_flavours` unit test and `in_out_parity_property` proptest are tautological: KI + KO = KI + (vanilla - KI) = vanilla holds algebraically regardless of whether the RR block selection is correct. The test docstring even claims parity 'is the headline cross-check' — it is not a cross-check at all.
findings.why_it_matters: A reviewer reading the suite would believe barrier correctness is validated by parity, but parity cannot detect an error in the RrBlocks A..D formulas or the regime selection. The real validation lives elsewhere (the QuantLib golden grid), so the in-crate suite overstates its own coverage.
findings.recommended_fix: Either compute KO directly from its own RR block combination and assert KO+KI=vanilla as a genuine independent check, or rewrite the test docstrings to state plainly that parity is structural and that the independent validation is the celnet-golden QuantLib grid. Add at least one in-crate hard-coded reference price for a KI flavour so the block formulas are checked without leaving the crate.

findings.location: crates/celnet-exotics/src/touch.rs (whole module); crates/celnet-golden/data (only barrier_gk.csv, digital_gk.csv, vanilla_gk.csv)
findings.issue: One-touch/no-touch, double-no-touch, double-touch and the double-barrier knock-out have NO independent external (QuantLib/published) reference validation. Their tests only assert internal self-consistency (complementarity OT+NT=DF, DNT+DT=DF, bounds, monotonicity, series-truncation convergence against the SAME series) plus a coarse, self-written MC oracle (touch.rs:507, barrier.rs:634) with ~1e-2..1.5e-2 tolerance. Complementarity is structural (no_touch is defined as DF - one_touch, touch.rs:180-183; double_touch as DF - DNT, :338-341), so those identities are tautological like the barrier parity.
findings.why_it_matters: Touches and DNTs are flagship FX products with well-known closed forms QuantLib can produce. A sign or exponent error in the lambda/mu power weights, or a wrong reflection in the DNT image series, would pass every current test (the self-MC oracle is too noisy to catch a few-percent bias, and the complementarity checks cannot catch a common-mode error shared by OT and NT). This is the single weakest validation area in the lane.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a frozen golden CSV (one_touch/no_touch/DNT/double_touch/double-KO) generated from QuantLib and assert celnet matches at ~1e-7 relative, exactly as barrier_grid.rs does for single barriers.

findings.issue: The LSV window-barrier MC uses a hard 'median rule' indicator: a segment is declared crossed iff the Brownian-bridge crossing probability exp(-2(H-a)(H-b)/segvar) > 0.5. This is a biased estimator of the continuously-monitored barrier — it is NOT the unbiased conditional-survival expectation that the 1-D engine uses (mc.rs:182-189, where survival is accumulated as the continuous probability). The docstring's claim that 'prob > 1/2 ... matches the analytic continuous barrier in the refinement limit' is dubious: the median rule converges to the discrete-monitoring indicator as dt->0 (each segment's crossing prob ->0 interior), systematically UNDER-counting crossings and biasing the knockout price UP.
findings.why_it_matters: PDE-vs-MC agreement is the headline cross-engine guarantee for second-generation payoffs, but the MC leg carries a method bias the PDE does not. The test (lsv.rs:553) only passes because the tolerance is a loose 3*se + 2.5e-2 absolute on a ~small price; a real survivorship bias of O(1/sqrt(steps)) hides comfortably under it. Booking a window barrier off this MC would mis-mark.
findings.recommended_fix: Use the same continuous fractional-survival accumulation as mc.rs::barrier_payoff (multiply per-step bridge survival into a path weight) instead of a 0.5-threshold indicator, or apply the BGK shift to the monitored window level. Tighten the PDE-vs-MC tolerance once the bias is removed.

findings.issue: The outer far-field Dirichlet edges (node 0 and node n-1) are initialised to the terminal intrinsic max(phi(S-K),0) (line 104-107) and then NEVER updated during the backward time-stepping — `apply_dirichlet` only zeroes the knock-out wall side, and `interior_range` excludes the two outer nodes from the Thomas solve. For a vanilla/knock-out call the correct far-field value grows like S*df_for - K*df_dom, not the frozen undiscounted intrinsic; the RHS fold-in at :331-332 uses these stale edge values.
findings.why_it_matters: Freezing the boundary at the undiscounted intrinsic injects an O(discount) boundary error that only the 8-stdev domain width hides. It is a latent correctness bug: at higher rates, longer T, or narrower domains the PDE will drift from the analytic price, and any future caller who shrinks width_in_std to cut cost will silently lose accuracy. The cross-validation tests pass only because the domain is very wide.
findings.recommended_fix: Update the outer Dirichlet edges each step with the analytic far-field (e.g. discounted forward intrinsic S*df_for - K*df_dom for a call upper edge, 0 for the lower), or use a linearity (U_xx=0) boundary, rather than holding the terminal intrinsic constant for the whole solve.

findings.issue: The MC 'antithetic' reflects BOTH driving uniforms via 1-u for the s<0 twin. For the orthogonal spot normal this is a true antithetic (inverse_cdf(1-u) = -z). For the QE variance step it is not: in the squared-Gaussian branch v' = a(b+z)^2 is not symmetric under z->-z (unless b=0), so the twin path follows a DIFFERENT variance trajectory rather than a reflected one. The pairing therefore does not cleanly cancel the odd component of the variance-driven part of the payoff.
findings.why_it_matters: Variance reduction from the antithetic is weaker than the docstring implies ('keeps the pair exactly variance-reducing'), and the reported std_error understates true error less than expected. Not a bias (each path is still a valid draw), but the claimed property is overstated and the estimator is less efficient than a true antithetic.
findings.recommended_fix: Document that the variance leg's antithetic is approximate, or draw the variance with a sign-flippable representation (e.g. carry an explicit Gaussian z_var and use 1-u only on the orthogonal leg) so the spot's correlated part is genuinely reflected.

findings.issue: The 128-bit counter high word is built by an ad-hoc mix `((stream<<32) ^ path).rotate_left(17) ^ (path<<1)` rather than placing (stream, path) into disjoint counter lanes as the counter-based-RNG design intends. This is not the canonical coordinate->counter mapping and could, for adversarial path-index patterns, alias two distinct (stream,path) tuples into the same hi word (the key also folds stream via XOR at :102, which mitigates but does not guarantee injectivity).
findings.why_it_matters: The whole point of a counter-based generator is a provably-injective coordinate map giving independent substreams. An ad-hoc bijection undermines the 'statistically independent yet reproducible' guarantee the docstring makes; collisions would correlate paths and bias the estimator. The `distinct_coordinates_differ` test only checks a handful of tuples, not injectivity.
findings.recommended_fix: Map path into the low-counter high lane and stream into the key only (or use a full 64-bit path lane), keeping the (stream,path,step,draw) partition strictly disjoint and obviously injective; add a test that sweeps many path indices for first-block collisions.

findings.issue: The 'calibrated LSV reprices the surface' guarantee is tested only at a single ATM strike (1.30 / forward) with a 2e-2..3e-2 absolute tolerance, and the surface-end-to-end test uses a flat or mild SVI surface. There is no test that the calibrated LSV reprices the smile WINGS (off-ATM strikes) — which is the entire purpose of the leverage calibration. A leverage surface that is wrong away from the money would pass.
findings.why_it_matters: Repricing the surface is headline guarantee #1 (lsv.rs:36). Validating only ATM, where leverage ~ 1 by construction for a flat input, does not exercise the Dupire/particle machinery's actual job (matching skew/convexity). This overstates the calibration's validated scope.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a repricing test across multiple strikes (e.g. 10d/25d put and call) against the input surface's Black prices, with a tolerance appropriate to the particle/ADI discretisation, on a genuinely skewed+convex surface.

findings.issue: Several closed forms silently clamp to absorb numerical defects: dnt_survival clamps the image series into [0,1] AND then caps it by an independently-computed single-wall bound (a fallback that masks series breakdown rather than fixing it), and double_knock_out_price applies (phi*sum).max(0.0). The DKO is NOT clamped to <= vanilla and has no upper guard; the clamps elsewhere can hide a genuinely diverging/incorrect series in 'stiff extreme-drift corners' (the code's own words).
findings.why_it_matters: Clamping turns a wrong number into a plausible-but-wrong number, defeating detection. The DNT cap-by-single-wall is doing real correctness work for some regimes, which means the raw image series is not trustworthy there — yet there is no golden test to bound how wrong it can be before the cap engages.
findings.recommended_fix: Add asserts/diagnostics (in debug) when the clamp or cap actually binds, and add golden DNT/DKO references covering the stiff-drift regimes so the clamp is proven to be cosmetic rather than load-bearing.

findings.issue: Image-series truncation counts are fixed compile-time constants. The convergence test (touch.rs:460) only compares 12 terms vs 200 terms of the SAME series on two benign corridors; it does not establish that 10/12 terms suffice for tight corridors or extreme drift, where geometric convergence slows (ratio ~ corridor width in log-space). For a very tight corridor relative to vol*sqrt(T), more reflections are needed.
findings.why_it_matters: A fixed term count that is adequate for the tested corridors may be insufficient for the tight DNT/DKO corridors that are common in FX (e.g. 1-week 5%-wide DNTs), producing a truncation error the clamps then hide. Scale/robustness for the full product range is not demonstrated.
findings.recommended_fix: Either derive the term count from the corridor-width-to-stdev ratio with a proven error bound, or test convergence on the tightest corridors the product supports and document the validated range.

findings.issue: box_muller calls libm::cos/libm::sin directly rather than routing through celnet_core::math, unlike every other transcendental in the crate. CLAUDE.md mandates 'Every transcendental routes through celnet_core::math'. The crate even adds a direct libm dependency in Cargo.toml solely for this.
findings.why_it_matters: It bypasses the project's single math-abstraction seam. While libm is still deterministic, the rule exists so the determinism contract has one chokepoint; a future swap of celnet-core's trig backend would silently not apply here, and the crate-level doc (lib.rs:76-79) claims 'Every transcendental routes through celnet_core::math', which is now inaccurate.
findings.recommended_fix: Add sin/cos to celnet_core::math and route box_muller through it (dropping the direct libm dep), or update the crate doc to acknowledge the trig exception with the libm justification.

findings.location: crates/celnet-exotics/src/mc.rs (no quasi-MC / Sobol), src/lsv.rs (no LSV Greeks)
findings.issue: State-of-the-art FX exotics engines provide (a) Sobol/Brownian-bridge quasi-Monte-Carlo for variance-optimal convergence on barriers/Asians, and (b) pathwise/adjoint (AAD) or at least bumped Greeks for the LSV book. This crate has only pseudo-random Philox MC and exposes no Greeks for the LSV/PDE/MC layer (digitals have closed-form Greeks; barriers/touches/LSV do not).
findings.why_it_matters: Against the competition (the audit asks for >= Synoption/Fenics/Bloomberg) a booking model without exotic Greeks and without QMC is not production-complete: a desk cannot risk-manage barriers/DNTs/LSV trades from price alone, and 1/sqrt(N) MC is too slow for an IB-sized book at the latency budgets the project mandates.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a Sobol sequence + Brownian-bridge path construction (the doc already name-drops bridge-friendly inverse-CDF), and expose bucketed/AAD Greeks for the barrier/touch/LSV layer.

findings.issue: Second-generation coverage stops at window/partial single barriers and double knock-OUT. There is no double-knock-in, no KIKO, no double-no-touch-on-LSV, no Asian on the LSV engine, no forward-start/cliquet, and the LSV PDE handles only single-wall knock-outs (double-barrier on the 2-D ADI is absent). The arithmetic Asian exists only in the flat-vol MC.
findings.why_it_matters: The lane brief and competitive bar imply a full first/second-generation exotic surface. The missing structures (double KIKO, DKI, LSV-priced touches/DNTs) are standard FX desk inventory; their absence is a real capability gap vs incumbents.
findings.recommended_fix: Extend the ADI grid to a two-wall (corridor) Dirichlet layout and add the missing knock-in / double-barrier / touch payoffs on the LSV engines, with cross-validation against the flat-vol analytics in the local-vol limit.

overall: The exotics crate is genuinely substantial and largely correct: it implements all 8 single barriers + double-KO, the full touch/DNT/double-touch family, cash/asset digitals with closed-form Greeks, a CN+Rannacher 1-D PDE, a Philox/Brownian-bridge/BGK/control-variate MC, and a complete LSV stack (QE variance + Dupire-w-form local vol + interacting-particle leverage + Hundsdorfer-Verwer ADI). Determinism discipline is strong (counter-based RNG, libm everywhere except one box_muller trig call, only one harmless `rebate == 0.0` float-equality guard, no NaN asserts, no FMA), all identifiers are vendor/research-neutral with provenance confined to doc comments, and there are no commercial deps or versioned APIs. Single barriers and digitals ARE independently validated against a frozen QuantLib 1.42.1 golden grid (288 barrier rows at 1e-9 relative), which materially de-risks the analytic core. The most important weaknesses are validation-shaped rather than outright wrong-formula: (1) the in/out parity 'cross-check' for barriers and the complementarity 'checks' for touches/DNT are structural tautologies, not independent validation; (2) touches/DNT/double-touch/double-KO have NO external golden reference at all (only self-consistency + a noisy self-written MC) — the single biggest gap; (3) the LSV window-barrier MC uses a biased 0.5-threshold bridge indicator that does not match the PDE's continuous-survival treatment; (4) the 1-D PDE freezes its far-field Dirichlet edges at the undiscounted terminal intrinsic for the whole solve, a latent boundary error hidden only by a wide domain. Plus several minors (approximate variance antithetic mis-described as exact, ad-hoc Philox counter mixing, ATM-only surface-repricing test, clamp/cap masking of image-series breakdown) and capability gaps vs the competitive bar (no QMC/Sobol, no exotic/LSV Greeks, no DKI/KIKO/LSV-touches). None are correctness blockers given the QuantLib golden coverage of the analytic single-barrier/digital core, but the touch/DNT validation gap and the window-barrier MC bias should be closed before this is trusted for booking.

area: celnet-gpu (PricingBackend / wgpu f32 + f64 CPU reconciliation / Philox) and celnet-engine (zero-alloc hot core, rtrb SPSC, arc-swap/seqlock, blue-green handoff)

findings.issue: The single-writer seqlock copies the payload with plain non-atomic accesses on both sides: the writer does `*self.value.get() = value;` (line 217-219) while a reader concurrently does `let value = unsafe { *self.value.get() };` (line 241). These two non-atomic accesses to the same `UnsafeCell<T>` are unsynchronized (the reader only discovers the conflict *after* it has already performed the read, via the post-read sequence check), so they form a data race that is undefined behavior under the C++20/Rust memory model — even for `T: Copy`. The sequence-number protocol guarantees the *result* is discarded, but the model does not permit the racing read to occur at all; the compiler is free to assume it never happens and miscompile (e.g. tear the load across the sequence checks, hoist it, or produce a trap value). The SAFETY comment claims 'this is a plain bitwise copy with no aliasing of a live &mut' — that is exactly the racy access the model forbids.
findings.why_it_matters: Guardrail #2/#5 demand 100%-correct, gate-passing code; this is latent UB on the most safety-critical primitive in the hot path (it would also be flagged by ThreadSanitizer/Miri). It works today only by the grace of the optimizer; a future rustc/LLVM version can break it silently. This is the textbook reason real seqlocks (the `seqlock` crate, Folly SeqLock, Linux READ_ONCE) never use a plain field copy.
findings.recommended_fix: Do not copy `T` with a plain read/write. Either (a) store the payload as a fixed array of `AtomicU64`/`AtomicU8` (or `[MaybeUninit<u8>; size_of::<T>()]` copied via `ptr::read_volatile`/`copy_nonoverlapping` between `compiler_fence`s) so the per-word accesses are not data races, or (b) depend on the audited `seqlock` crate. Update the SAFETY comment to reflect the volatile/atomic copy protocol that actually makes it sound.

findings.issue: The 'real GPU f32 vs f64 CPU reconciliation bound' (5e-4) is an empirical constant measured once on M4 Metal, not a derived or per-adapter-verified guarantee. WGSL `exp`/`log`/`cos`/`sqrt` have implementation-defined precision (the WebGPU spec only mandates loose ULP bounds that vary per backend/driver), so the GPU f32 path is NOT bit-reproducible across adapters and the agreement with the CPU oracle can differ substantially between Vulkan/DX12/GLES/Metal drivers and across paths sitting near the strike (where a small z perturbation flips in/out of the money). Worse, in headless CI (no adapter) `GpuBackend::new()` falls back to the f64 `CpuBackend`, so `r_gpu` becomes bit-identical to `r_cpu` and the reconciliation assertion (line 413) is vacuously satisfied — the bound is never exercised anywhere except a developer's M4.
findings.why_it_matters: The crate's headline claim is 'f32 GPU + f64 CPU reconciliation bounds the error.' That bound is asserted nowhere in CI and is an un-proven magic number elsewhere; a driver whose transcendentals are weaker than Metal's could silently exceed 5e-4 and ship wrong prices. This undercuts the determinism/validation pillar (guardrail #5/#6).
findings.recommended_fix: Gate the reconciliation assertion on `gpu.is_gpu()` (skip-with-warning, don't pass vacuously, when falling back). Derive the bound from first principles (per-path f32 ULP propagation through GBM+payoff, divided by sqrt(N) for the mean) and assert that derived bound, or add a Lavapipe/software-Vulkan CI job so a real non-Metal f32 path is exercised. Soften the lib.rs claim to 'bounded on tested adapters' until a cross-adapter bound exists.

findings.issue: The zero-allocation proof only covers the single-threaded, no-concurrent-publish case. The hot `price()` path calls `self.state.load()` -> `ArcSwap::load_full()` (rt.rs:104), which is documented as 'a refcount bump, not a heap allocation' — true on the uncontended fast path, but `arc-swap`'s `load_full` is not unconditionally allocation-free under concurrent `store()` (its debt-list / generation reclamation can fall back to slower paths). The zero_alloc test (no writer thread runs during the measured window) never exercises a concurrent `publish()`, so the asserted property is narrower than the lib.rs claim that 'the hot path never allocates' while market ticks/recalibrations are being published.
findings.why_it_matters: Guardrail #6 makes zero-alloc a hard requirement, and the real production scenario is exactly load-under-concurrent-publish (a market tick lands while the core is pricing). The proof as written does not cover that scenario, so the claim is overstated relative to what is tested.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a zero_alloc variant with a concurrent publisher thread hammering `state().publish()` during the measured pricing window, and assert the allocation count still does not move. If `load_full` cannot be guaranteed alloc-free under contention, switch the read side to `ArcSwap::load()` (a `Guard`, no strong-count clone) held only for the pricing arithmetic, and document the precise guarantee.

findings.issue: The crate advertises a 'core-pinned busy-poll pricing core' and the audit target includes 'shutdown always terminates', but the engine crate contains no driver loop, no spawned core thread, and no shutdown/stop mechanism. It only exposes `PricingCore::drain` (one bounded poll) plus `pin_current_thread_to_core`. The actual busy-poll loop + lifecycle/shutdown lives elsewhere (celnet-server). There is therefore no shutdown logic in this crate to verify, and the lib.rs module doc describing 'busy-poll pricing core' overstates what the crate itself provides.
findings.why_it_matters: A reviewer (and operator) reading celnet-engine would expect the run/stop lifecycle here; its absence means the 'never blocks / always terminates' guarantees are unowned at this layer and depend entirely on the server wiring being correct. Docs/code drift violates guardrail #10.
findings.recommended_fix: Either provide the owned busy-poll driver (a `run(stop: &AtomicBool)`/handle with a documented, race-free shutdown that drains and joins) inside celnet-engine with a bounded shutdown test, or correct the module docs to state the crate provides only the lock-free primitives and one-shot `drain`, with the loop/shutdown owned by celnet-server.

findings.issue: `PathSpec.steps` is documented as advancing the Philox `step` coordinate for path-dependent extensions, and `gbm()` clamps it to `>= 1`, but both the CPU `terminal_spot` (`rng.normal(p, 0, 0)`) and the WGSL kernel (`philox_normal(path, 0u, 0u)`) hardcode step 0 and ignore `steps` entirely. The field is dead for anything but a single exact GBM terminal.
findings.why_it_matters: The doc implies multi-step/path-dependent capability that does not exist; a caller setting steps>1 silently gets a single-step terminal. Minor today (only vanilla terminals are priced) but it is a latent correctness trap and a docs-vs-code mismatch (guardrail #10).
findings.recommended_fix: Either remove `steps` until the multi-step engine exists, or implement the per-step Euler/exact loop that consumes `rng.normal(p, step, 0)` for each step on both CPU and WGSL. Update the doc to match whichever is chosen.

findings.issue: No GPU-path test exercises a path count that is not an exact multiple of WG_SIZE. The reconciliation test uses 256*4096 (exact) and the only non-multiple count (100_000) goes through the forced CPU fallback. The shader's `if (path < params.paths)` partial-workgroup guard and the host `div_ceil(...).max(1)` group count are thus never validated on a real device for the ragged-tail case.
findings.why_it_matters: An off-by-one in the tail guard would bias the Monte-Carlo mean (extra zero/garbage payoffs) and would not be caught. Scale/IB-sized batches will routinely have non-aligned path counts.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a GPU reconciliation test (gated on is_gpu) with a deliberately ragged path count (e.g. 1_000_003) and assert it still matches the CPU oracle within the bound and that the path count is honored exactly.

findings.issue: Beyond the data-race blocker above, the store's first sequence transition (load Relaxed at 210, store odd Relaxed at 211) reads then writes non-atomically; this is only safe because of the single-writer contract, which is documented but not enforced or debug-asserted. A second accidental writer (e.g. a future refactor sharing the Seqlock) would silently corrupt the protocol with no diagnostic.
findings.why_it_matters: The soundness of the whole primitive rests on an unchecked invariant. A cheap guard converts a silent corruption into a loud failure during tests.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a `debug_assert!` writer-token / single-writer guard (e.g. an `AtomicBool` taken at store entry under `debug_assertions`) so a contract violation is caught in tests, and keep the type `!Sync`-for-writing by handing out a single owned writer handle from `PricingCore`.

findings.issue: `ctx.device.poll(wgpu::PollType::wait_indefinitely())` plus `rx.recv()` after `map_async` will block forever if the device is lost or the queue stalls — there is no timeout or device-lost handling. The surrounding code uses `.expect(...)` which would only fire on an explicit error result, not on an indefinite hang.
findings.why_it_matters: On a production GPU a device-lost/hang would wedge the calling thread permanently with no recovery, contradicting the platform's mission-critical/always-terminates posture. (This is init/off-hot-path, so severity is limited.)
findings.recommended_fix: Use a bounded poll/timeout loop (poll with a deadline) and surface a device-lost/timeout error that triggers a clean fallback to the CPU oracle, rather than blocking indefinitely.

findings.issue: The backend is limited to single-asset GBM European vanilla terminals (one exact step, Box-Muller cosine branch only, no antithetic/control-variate variance reduction, no Sobol/QMC despite the task/ledger mentioning 'Philox/Sobol', no path-dependent/barrier MC, no multi-asset, no Greeks via pathwise/AD on GPU). The CPU 'oracle' is itself a 4M-path MC, not a closed-form/QuantLib golden reference for the reconciliation.
findings.why_it_matters: State-of-the-art FX-options MC engines (and the competition) provide QMC/Sobol with Brownian-bridge, variance reduction, and at least barrier/touch payoffs plus pathwise Greeks; vanilla-only GBM with crude pseudo-random MC is well below the bar the platform claims (guardrail #6, competitive positioning).
findings.recommended_fix: Add Sobol/QMC with a deterministic scrambling, antithetic/control-variate variance reduction, GPU pathwise/likelihood-ratio Greeks, and at least barrier/touch payoff kernels; and reconcile the GPU price against the closed-form Garman-Kohlhagen (already available in celnet-vanilla) as the golden oracle rather than only against another MC.

findings.issue: The SPSC ring transport is a single fixed-capacity (4096) edge<->core pair with no batching API, no NUMA/affinity-aware multi-core fan-out, and a single pricing core that prices one request at a time through a scalar closed form. There is no path to the GPU/SIMD batch backend from the hot core, and no multi-core or sharded-book scale-out.
findings.why_it_matters: Guardrail #6 requires investment-banking-sized portfolios and HFT streaming throughput; a single scalar core behind one 4096-slot ring is a throughput ceiling far below that and does not exercise the GPU batch engine that the same workspace ships.
findings.recommended_fix: Provide a batched request/response path (price N strikes per poll), a multi-core sharded engine (per-shard ring + book partition), and a documented bridge from the hot core to the celnet-gpu batch backend for large repricings, with a throughput benchmark validating the §1.2 budget.

overall: Both crates are real, non-mock implementations with thoughtful determinism discipline (counter-based Philox with known-answer vectors, libm-routed transcendentals, integer/pairwise reductions never float atomics, CachePadded counters, an honest single-threaded zero-alloc proof). The Philox CPU/WGSL parity, the byte-exact handoff serializer, and the arc-swap publication are sound. However the central audited unsafe primitive — the seqlock — performs the payload copy with plain non-atomic reads/writes that race the writer, which is formal UB under the Rust/C++ memory model (BLOCKER): the protocol discards torn results but the racing access itself is disallowed and would trip Miri/TSan. The GPU 'f32 vs f64 reconciliation bound' is an empirical M4-only constant that is never exercised in headless CI (the assertion is vacuous when it falls back to the f64 CPU path) and is not derived or cross-adapter-verified, so the headline error guarantee is overstated. The zero-alloc proof omits the concurrent-publish scenario that matters in production. The crate also has no owned busy-poll driver or shutdown, so the lane's 'shutdown always terminates' requirement is unowned here and lives in celnet-server. Finally, the MC engine is vanilla-GBM-only (no Sobol/QMC, variance reduction, barriers, or GPU Greeks) and the hot core is single-scalar behind one ring — both below the state-of-the-art/IB-scale bar the platform claims. Fix the seqlock UB and the reconciliation/zero-alloc test coverage before this is 'done' per the project gates.

area: celnet-proto wire contract + celnet-server edge (RFQ/RFS/surface/scenario, core bridge) + celnet-client typed SDK (gap-detect/resync/reconnect)

findings.issue: AcceptQuote ignores the QuoteAccept.idempotency_key entirely. The accept is keyed only on quote_id; the request-supplied idempotency_key is never compared to the stored QuoteRecord's key. The proto doc (celnet.proto:513) and the module doc both promise the key makes accept-retries safe and request-matched, but any client knowing a quote_id can accept it with any (or empty) key, and an accept-retry is deduplicated purely by the already-booked execution, not by key match. The audit lane explicitly requires 'request-matched idempotency'; RequestQuote enforces an instrument/conventions match (idempotency_record_matches) but AcceptQuote enforces no match at all.
findings.why_it_matters: Contract drift between the documented request-matched idempotency guarantee and the implementation, plus a real authorization/safety gap: a stray or malicious accept on a borrowed quote_id books a trade. On a two-way quote an accept also carries a side; a retry with a *different* side silently returns the first booking, so a client that meant to flip side gets a wrong fill with no error.
findings.recommended_fix: Validate acc.idempotency_key against rec.quote.idempotency_key (reject mismatch with InvalidArgument, mirroring idempotency_conflict). On an already-booked quote, only return the stored execution when the retry's key AND side match; otherwise return FailedPrecondition/InvalidArgument rather than a mismatched booking.

findings.issue: RejectQuote performs no idempotency-key / requester match: it cancels a quote purely by quote_id (QuoteReject carries no key at all — celnet.proto:521-526). Combined with the accept gap, any party can decline another party's live quote. There is also no link between who requested the quote and who may reject/accept it.
findings.why_it_matters: A quote is a tradable commitment; allowing an unrelated caller to reject (or accept) it by guessing/observing a monotonically-assigned quote_id (next_quote_id starts at 1 and increments — trivially enumerable) is a denial-of-trade and mis-book vector. quote_id being a dense monotonic counter makes enumeration easy.
findings.recommended_fix: Add an idempotency_key (or session/owner token) to QuoteReject and bind reject/accept to the originating key. At minimum, make quote_id unguessable (random/HMAC) so it cannot be enumerated, and document the trust model.

findings.issue: When the gap predates the retained replay buffer, the fresh recovery snapshot is priced against sub.base_market (the fixed subscription-open spot), not the current deterministically-ticked spot (sub.tick produces the live path). The very next live drive_tick then reprices at sub.tick.next_spot(), so the resync snapshot baseline and the immediately-following Update are priced on different spots. The client applies the snapshot as its whole baseline (rfs.rs:349 sets last_seq=s.sequence and emits StreamEvent::Snapshot), so the consumer briefly holds an off-path price.
findings.why_it_matters: A resync is supposed to hand the client a known-good baseline it can apply whole; here the baseline is internally inconsistent with the very next tick (price/greeks jump for no market reason). Sequencing stays correct (no gap/dup), but the recovered price line is wrong for one step — a data-correctness defect a market-data consumer would flag.
findings.recommended_fix: Price the fresh resync snapshot against the subscription's current ticked market (advance/peek sub.tick consistently, or snapshot the last emitted Update's market), so the baseline matches the resumed live path. Make the snapshot reflect the same spot the next Update will continue from.

findings.issue: A per-subscription pricing error inside drive_tick sends an Err(Status) frame on the bidirectional stream and then marks the subscription lagged. But the client driver (rfs.rs:283-286) treats ANY Some(Err(status)) from the inbound stream as terminal: it emits the error and returns, killing the whole subscription/driver. So a transient/per-instrument pricing error on the server (recoverable, server-side) is unrecoverable on the client side, contradicting the server's 'recoverable, just this subscription' intent.
findings.why_it_matters: Server and client disagree on the recoverability of a mid-stream Status: the server keeps the subscription registered expecting a resync, the client tears down. A consumer loses the whole stream on a single bad tick.
findings.recommended_fix: Either do not surface per-subscription pricing errors as stream-level Err frames (carry them as a typed in-band event the client can ignore/resync on), or have the client distinguish recoverable per-subscription status from fatal transport status and resync instead of returning.

findings.issue: CoreLink::stop() calls core.join()/router.join() (blocking) and is invoked both explicitly and from Drop. main() runs under the default multi-threaded #[tokio::main] and calls link.stop() after edge.shutdown, which is fine, but the Drop impl will block a runtime worker thread on join() if a CoreLink is ever dropped on a current-thread runtime or inside an async task. The module docs call out the current-thread hazard for the response router but the blocking-join-in-Drop-on-an-async-thread footgun is not guarded.
findings.why_it_matters: A blocking join() executed on a tokio worker (e.g. CoreLink dropped within an async context on a single-threaded runtime, which several tests use) can deadlock the very runtime that must drive the threads being joined to completion. It works today only because of how main/tests happen to drop it.
findings.recommended_fix: Make Drop best-effort non-blocking (signal shutdown + detach), or document/assert that stop() must be called from a blocking context and Drop only signals. Consider join via spawn_blocking when on a runtime.

findings.issue: Doc comment states ServiceState '— mirrors the proto ServiceState', but celnet.proto defines no ServiceState message/enum (grep confirms none). The proto carries readiness only implicitly via Status::unavailable. Stale/overstated doc claim.
findings.why_it_matters: Project rule 10 mandates docs match code with no stale references; an audit reader is misled into expecting a wire ServiceState that does not exist, and a future change might 'restore' a nonexistent contract element.
findings.recommended_fix: Drop the 'mirrors the proto ServiceState' clause (it is an internal edge state machine), or add the ServiceState to the contract if a wire readiness signal is intended.

findings.issue: Two float comparisons in non-test production code use ad-hoc tolerances rather than celnet_core::is_close: surface.rs:170 `(d - 0.50).abs() < f64::EPSILON` to detect the ATM pillar, and surface_vocab.rs:203 `(p.delta - delta).abs() < 1e-9` to match a delta pillar. The determinism guardrail mandates all float compares go through is_close/assert_close.
findings.why_it_matters: Consistency with the stated discipline and reviewability. f64::EPSILON (~2.2e-16) is far tighter than the value's scale (0.5) and is effectively an exact match on a literal; if REPORT_DELTAS ever carries a computed (not literal) 0.50, the ATM branch silently stops firing and the strike falls back to forward via unwrap_or — a latent correctness trap.
findings.recommended_fix: Use celnet_core::is_close with explicit rel/abs tolerances for both pillar lookups; for the ATM detection key off an explicit marker (e.g. an enum pillar id) rather than a float equality on 0.50.

findings.location: crates/celnet-server/src/services/stream.rs:300-326 (session driver) and the absence of a server-side max-subscriptions / max-sessions bound
findings.issue: Each gRPC session spawns one driver task holding an unbounded HashMap<u64, Subscription>; there is no cap on subscriptions per session nor sessions per process, and each Subscription retains up to REPLAY_DEPTH=512 ServerStreamMessages (each carrying a full Greeks set). A client can Subscribe with arbitrarily many distinct subscription ids and grow memory unbounded; QuoteStore (quote.rs:80-84) is likewise unbounded with a comment acknowledging 'a production edge expires old quotes' but no expiry implemented.
findings.why_it_matters: The audit lane requires investment-banking-scale and 'edge never blocking the core'; the edge itself has unbounded growth surfaces (subscription map, replay buffers, quote store) that a single misbehaving or hostile session can exploit to OOM the edge. The TICK_INTERVAL of 5 ms per session also caps throughput well below an HFT budget for many sessions.
findings.recommended_fix: Cap subscriptions per session and total sessions; implement quote-record TTL/expiry (the validity deadline already exists — sweep expired records); make REPLAY_DEPTH memory accounted. Reconsider the fixed 5 ms tick vs an event/feed-driven update for production scale.

findings.issue: Scenario reprices each shocked node via price_instrument against a WireMarketContext whose `vol` is the shocked flat vol; price_instrument uses market.vol directly for the leg (pricer.rs:218 inputs_at(..., market.vol)). There is no smile re-evaluation under a spot shock: a spot shock keeps the same flat vol rather than rolling along the calibrated smile (sticky-strike/sticky-delta). Likewise RFQ/RFS price every instrument at snap.atm_vol (quote.rs:137-143, stream.rs:366-372) — the ATM vol at the forward — not the smile vol at the instrument's own strike, so off-ATM strikes are mispriced relative to the calibrated surface the SurfaceService exposes.
findings.why_it_matters: A desk what-if and an off-ATM RFQ that ignore the skew/smile are materially wrong vs Synoption/Fenics/Bloomberg, which reprice along the surface. The platform calibrates a Vanna-Volga smile (SurfaceService) but the quote/stream/scenario hot paths do not consult it for the strike being priced, so a 25-delta or barrier quote uses ATM vol — a real numerical-correctness gap vs state-of-the-art.
findings.recommended_fix: Resolve the per-strike (and per-shocked-spot) vol from the calibrated smile via CoreLink::surface_vol for every priced leg in RFQ/RFS/Scenario, and define an explicit sticky-strike vs sticky-delta convention for spot shocks. At minimum document that current pricing is flat-ATM-vol so it is not mistaken for surface-consistent.

findings.issue: The RFQ/RFS contract has no way to request a quote/stream under an explicit market or a named surface_version; the maker always prices against its own live state (documented intent). MarkSurfaceResponse returns a surface_version (proto:801) but no other message references it — a Quote/Snapshot cannot state which surface_version it was priced on, and there is no request field to pin a version. Quantity/Side are carried but RFQ ignores notional in pricing (premium is per-unit; no notional-scaled premium returned).
findings.why_it_matters: Auditable pricing and reproducibility: a counterparty cannot tie an executed Quote to the exact surface_version it was struck on, and cannot request a re-quote on a specific surface. This is on the explicit v2 roadmap (task #20: surface streaming/versioning) but is a current gap vs competitors that stamp marks with a surface revision.
findings.recommended_fix: Stamp Quote/Snapshot/PriceResponse with the surface_version they were priced against, and allow an optional surface_version pin on QuoteRequest/Subscribe/ScenarioRequest. Decide whether premium should also be returned notional-scaled.

findings.issue: Lag recovery relies on REPLAY_DEPTH (512) > CHANNEL_DEPTH (256): once a subscriber lags, it is paused and the LAGGED marker retried until a slot frees. But if the client never resyncs (e.g. it ignores LAGGED), the subscription stays registered forever in the lagged state, retaining its replay buffer and being re-walked every tick (drive_tick iterates all subs including paused ones). There is no abandonment timeout for a never-resynced lagged subscription.
findings.why_it_matters: A stalled or misbehaving consumer permanently retains server-side state and consumes a per-tick iteration slot; combined with no per-session subscription cap this compounds the unbounded-growth concern. The 'edge never blocking the core' holds (good — try_send, no block), but edge resource cleanup is incomplete.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a lag/abandonment deadline: if a lagged subscription is not resynced within N ticks/seconds, emit a terminal StreamEnd and remove it. Skip paused subs cheaply (separate paused set) so they do not cost a per-tick walk.

findings.issue: On a LAGGED StreamEnd the client resyncs on the SAME stream using last_seq. The server, however, only emits LAGGED after dropping updates whose sequences were never advanced/retained (good), but the client's GapDetected event it synthesizes uses last_good == observed == *last_seq (rfs.rs:420-423), which is not actually a gap — it is a 'you were dropped' signal. Reusing GapDetected{last_good==observed} overloads the event with a degenerate value a consumer cannot interpret.
findings.why_it_matters: Ergonomics/observability: a consumer watching GapDetected for monitoring sees a 'gap' with last_good==observed that did not correspond to any missed sequence, muddying lag vs gap telemetry.
findings.recommended_fix: Introduce a distinct StreamEvent::Lagged (or a reason field on GapDetected) so a consumer can distinguish a server-side drop-and-resync from a true client-detected sequence gap.

findings.issue: Server heartbeats are only emitted on the tick path when subs is non-empty and seq % HEARTBEAT_EVERY == 0 (a multiple of the advancing update sequence). If a subscription is lagged/paused (no sequence advance) or the tick produces only heartbeats, no liveness heartbeat is sent for that subscription at all; and an idle session with zero subscriptions emits nothing. The contract advertises heartbeats as the liveness mechanism (proto:597-608) but a paused or idle subscription gets none.
findings.why_it_matters: A client relying on heartbeats for liveness/timeout on a paused (lagged) or quiescent subscription will see silence and may treat the connection as dead, triggering needless reconnects — the opposite of the heartbeat's purpose.
findings.recommended_fix: Emit a time-based heartbeat per active subscription independent of update cadence (including while lagged/paused), and consider a session-level keepalive when no subscriptions are active.

overall: The lane is well-engineered and largely matches its documented contract: the wire schema is genuinely unversioned (no schema_version, confirmed in proto + ADR-0007 comment), identifiers are vendor/research-neutral in public APIs (provenance only in doc comments / test-fn names / out-of-lane surface types), and every async test is hard timeout-bounded (TEST_DEADLINE/STEP_DEADLINE wrappers throughout). The core-bridge design is sound: the hot pricing ring stays SPSC, the edge fans in/out via channels, the response router lives on a dedicated OS thread (with a well-reasoned justification for why a tokio task would wedge the current-thread scheduler), and the edge never blocks the core (all stream sends are try_send / bounded, lag is a recoverable pause not a core stall) — I found no deadlock that the edge can impose on the core. RFS resync is sequence-correct: the replay window seq>last_sequence plus the client's is_stale dedup yields no gaps and no duplicates across the lagged-recovery and clean-resync paths (the two server-side regression tests verify this). The most important defects are not in sequencing but in (1) idempotency/authorization on the RFQ accept/reject path — AcceptQuote ignores the idempotency_key it documents as request-matched and RejectQuote/Accept are keyed only on an enumerable monotonic quote_id, so the 'request-matched idempotency' the lane asked me to verify is only half-implemented (RequestQuote matches, Accept/Reject do not); and (2) numerical fidelity — RFQ/RFS/Scenario price every leg at flat ATM vol rather than the calibrated smile vol at the instrument's own strike, and a spot shock does not roll along the surface, so off-ATM and what-if pricing is materially behind the surface the platform itself calibrates. Two resync/stream polish issues (off-path fresh-snapshot baseline price; client treating recoverable per-sub Status as fatal), a blocking-join-in-Drop footgun, unbounded edge state (subscriptions/replay/quote store with no TTL or caps), and a stale 'mirrors the proto ServiceState' doc round out the findings. No blocker-level correctness/determinism/safety break or hard-rule violation was found; the two majors on idempotency request-matching are the priority fixes for the lane's stated guarantees.

area: celnet-observability, celnet-integration, celnet-golden, celnet-bench, celnet-testkit, celnet-cli

findings.issue: The wire message carries a full convention descriptor (delta, atm, premium_in_foreign) but normalize() only cross-checks the DELTA convention against the resolved ConventionRecord. The ATM convention (msg.conventions.atm: WireAtmConvention) is decoded, never compared to resolved.atm, and silently dropped; premium_in_foreign is only checked for internal consistency with the declared delta, not against the resolved record. A feed declaring AtmForward where Celnet resolves DeltaNeutralStraddle passes and builds the surface with the wrong ATM strike.
findings.why_it_matters: The crate's headline claim (lib.rs:42 'Every delta/premium/cut choice goes through the resolved ConventionRecord; mislabelled feeds are rejected, not silently mispriced') is false for the ATM and cut dimensions. Convention error dwarfs model error in FX options — an ATM-convention mismatch mis-places the ATM pillar strike for the entire surface, exactly the silent mispricing the design says it prevents.
findings.recommended_fix: In normalize(), also assert msg.conventions.atm.canonical() == resolved.atm (and resolve/cross-check the cut/premium dimensions the ConventionRecord exposes), returning a new AtmConventionMismatch error variant on disagreement, symmetric to DeltaConventionMismatch.

findings.issue: normalize() computes vol-time t with a crude nominal map (Overnight 1/365, Weeks w*7/365, Months m*30/365, Years y*365/365) instead of the calendar-exact celnet_conventions::vol_year_fraction. A 3M slice gets t=90/365≈0.24658 rather than the true ACT/365F day count (~0.2493), a ~1% vol-time error; Months*30 ignores actual month lengths and Years ignores leap days.
findings.why_it_matters: This t flows into MarketContext and directly into the surface/smile and every priced option from the integration pipeline.
