A ~1% error in vol-time is a first-order pricing error that contradicts the 'convention-correct ingest' and 'honoured to machine precision' claims, and it is silent (no error, no flag). The exact function already exists in the same workspace.
findings.recommended_fix: Thread a horizon/valuation Date into the pipeline and message (the feed already carries observed_at_nanos) and use celnet_conventions::vol_year_fraction(pair, horizon, tenor). If no horizon is ever available, downgrade the docstrings that claim convention-correctness/exactness for vol-time and document the residual as a known approximation.

findings.issue: The crate doc claims it turns the microsecond budgets into 'reproducible proof' and the benches are described as proving 'p50 ≤ 2 µs' / '≥1M updates/s/core'. But nothing asserts the budget: divan only measures and prints; there is no test or gate that fails when p50 regresses above 2 µs or throughput drops below 1M/s. Benches are also not run by `just check`.
findings.why_it_matters: A latency 'gate that does not gate' is exactly the overstated-claim failure mode the audit targets. A regression that doubles hot-path latency would not fail CI; the 'proof' is purely advisory output a human must read. Guardrail #6 makes performance a requirement, not an afterthought, so the budget must be enforced, not narrated.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a budget-gating test (e.g. a #[test] that times representative_inputs/batch over many iterations and asserts the measured median/throughput against the documented budget with margin), or wire a divan threshold into a CI step that fails on regression. Until then, soften the 'reproducible proof' language to 'measurement harness'.

findings.issue: HotProbe.seq is incremented unconditionally (including on a dropped push, line 74), and on success publishes the seq value into `shared.published` (line 79). published() therefore returns the last successfully-stamped sequence, which after any drops equals (count_published + count_dropped at last success), NOT the count of published samples. The doc/method name say 'Number of samples successfully published so far'.
findings.why_it_matters: The counter over-reports successful publishes once the ring has ever dropped, so any operator dashboard or capacity calc reading published() (or published()-style deltas) will be wrong under exactly the backpressure conditions where the number matters most. It is currently diagnostic-only (no consumer found), limiting blast radius.
findings.recommended_fix: Either maintain a separate monotonic published-count atomic incremented only on Ok(()), or rename/redocument published() as 'last published sequence' and expose a true count separately. Keep seq monotonic-across-drops (the drain's gap detection depends on it) but stop conflating it with a success count.

findings.issue: SourceId stores up to 16 raw bytes of the source name and as_str() does from_utf8(..).unwrap_or("?"). Truncating at a fixed 16-byte boundary can split a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, making as_str() silently return "?" and losing attribution. Separately, two distinct source names sharing the same 16-byte prefix collide on the derive(PartialEq,Eq,Hash) over `bytes`, so the divergence/blend join (aggregate.rs `d.source == source`) would treat them as one source.
findings.why_it_matters: SourceId is the identity used to attribute divergence/staleness and to exclude an outlier feed from the blended mid. A collision or lost name silently mis-attributes which feed disagreed, or could exclude/keep the wrong source — a correctness issue in the fault-tolerance path the crate exists to provide.
findings.recommended_fix: Truncate on a char boundary (str::char_indices / floor to a valid boundary) so as_str() never yields "?", and either store a hash/longer id or document that source names must be unique within their first 16 bytes (and assert it) to prevent join collisions.

findings.issue: The 'robust median consensus with 50% breakdown point' degrades for small/even source counts. With exactly 2 sources the median equals the mean of the two, so a rogue source pulls the consensus halfway and both sources sit equidistant from it: neither can be flagged relative to the other (or both are), defeating outlier rejection precisely in the common dual-feed case. There is no minimum-source guard and no MAD-scaled threshold despite the doc citing Hampel/Rousseeuw-Croux MAD.
findings.why_it_matters: The blend's divergence gate is the mechanism that stops a single mispriced feed from poisoning the mid. With two feeds (a realistic FX setup) the gate cannot identify which of two disagreeing feeds is the outlier, so a stale/rogue feed is blended in at full weight. The doc oversells the robustness actually implemented (fixed absolute tolerance, not the cited MAD rule).
findings.recommended_fix: Document the dual-feed limitation explicitly and require N≥3 for meaningful gating, or implement the cited MAD-based rule (flag when |dev| > k·MAD) and add a path for the 2-source case (e.g. fall back to staleness-only weighting plus an explicit 'undecidable divergence' quality flag).

findings.issue: The single-barrier golden grid is generated with rebate=0.0 only. The rebate leg of single_barrier_price is therefore never validated against the QuantLib oracle; the README/test admit it is 'exercised separately by the exotics crate's own tests' — i.e. by Celnet's own (non-independent) tests, not the independent oracle.
findings.why_it_matters: The entire stated value of the barrier golden gate is being the INDEPENDENT oracle that catches errors the in-crate parity/relationship tests cannot. Rebate pricing (especially the at-hit vs at-expiry rebate discounting and the knock-out rebate on touch) is a classic source of sign/discounting bugs, and it currently has zero independent QuantLib coverage.
findings.recommended_fix: Extend generate.py to emit nonzero-rebate barrier rows (QuantLib's AnalyticBarrierEngine prices the rebate leg) across the flavours and add assertions in barrier_grid.rs so the rebate term is gated against the oracle.

findings.issue: Two independent parse_tenor implementations exist (celnet-cli and celnet-integration), each re-deriving ON/W/M/Y tenor-token parsing, with no canonical Tenor parser in celnet-types or celnet-conventions. They can (and do) differ in trimming/case/error handling.
findings.why_it_matters: Guardrail #10 mandates zero duplicate logic and a single source of truth; CLAUDE.md guardrail #8 puts the FX vocabulary in celnet-types. Divergent tenor parsers mean a token accepted at the CLI edge may be rejected (or parsed differently) at the integration edge, and a fix to one will silently leave the other stale.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a canonical Tenor::from_market_token (or FromStr) in celnet-types (or celnet-conventions) and have both celnet-cli and celnet-integration call it; delete the two local copies.

findings.issue: AuditDrain::try_commit/commit_blocking doc states records 'arrive strictly in the sequence order the sink assigned (FIFO on a single unbounded queue), so a committer can persist them as a totally ordered, gap-free stream' (lines 142-144, 169). But with concurrent cloned sinks the fetch_add(SeqCst) sequence assignment and the subsequent send() are not atomic together, so arrival order need not equal sequence order — a fact the struct's own field comment (lines 127-131) correctly acknowledges and tracks via highest_committed as a running max.
findings.why_it_matters: The method-level docs contradict the field-level docs and the actual behavior. A reader/compliance integrator who trusts 'persist them as a totally ordered, gap-free stream' directly from try_commit would persist out-of-order under concurrency and could mistake a transient out-of-order arrival for a gap. Losslessness holds; in-order delivery does not.
findings.recommended_fix: Correct the try_commit/commit_blocking docs to say arrival is FIFO-per-producer but global sequence order must be recovered downstream by sorting on AuditRecord.sequence (as the field doc already states), and ensure any 'gap-free' assertion is qualified as 'after sort/over the full drain'.

findings.issue: The 'known-BAD inputs must make the invariants FIRE' tests largely re-implement the helper's internal comparison (e.g. parity_fires_on_broken_relation, greek_oracle_fires_on_wrong_analytic, convexity_rejects_negative_butterfly) and assert on is_close directly rather than invoking the public assert_* helper and confirming it panics. Only two helpers (maturity precondition, convexity spacing) are exercised end-to-end via catch_unwind.
findings.why_it_matters: These tests can pass even if a refactor weakens or skips the assertion inside the public helper (e.g. an accidental early-return), because they never call the helper on the bad value. The suite's purpose — proving the invariant assertions actually fire — is only partially met.
findings.recommended_fix: Add catch_unwind-based negative tests that call the actual public helpers (assert_put_call_parity, assert_greek_matches_fd, assert_strike_convexity) on hand-built violating inputs/values and assert the result is Err (panicked), covering every assertion helper, not just two.

overall: The lane is high-quality and largely lives up to its claims, with two genuinely load-bearing proofs that hold up under scrutiny: the zero-alloc hot-path guard (counting global allocator + negative control, channel.rs publish does only a wait-free rtrb push + Relaxed store, HotSample is 32-byte POD) and the lossless-vs-lossy split (audit_channel unbounded + SeqCst gap-free sequence, telemetry ring drop-on-full). The golden gates are real: tools/goldgen/generate.py emits genuine QuantLib 1.42.1 GarmanKohlagenProcess prices/Greeks into frozen CSVs (no celnet self-column), and the three test files call celnet_vanilla/celnet_exotics directly and assert is_close against the oracle across a non-degenerate spot×moneyness×vol×maturity×rate×type grid, with per-flavour presence checks. HdrHistogram coordinated-omission uses record_correct correctly and is proven to inflate the tail. No commercial deps; deps are permissive OSS. No unsafe outside the audited test allocator; no float == in non-test lane code; no async tests (so the timeout rule is N/A) and the one wall-clock-bounded audit integration test has a hard DEADLINE. The defects cluster in celnet-integration (ATM/premium convention NOT cross-checked despite the headline claim; crude nominal vol-time instead of the existing calendar-exact vol_year_fraction; small/even-N divergence gate degeneracy; SourceId UTF-8 truncation + prefix-collision) and in overstated claims (celnet-bench advertises 'reproducible proof' of latency budgets but nothing gates them; audit docs overstate in-order delivery; golden barrier rebate leg has no independent oracle coverage). None of these are determinism/safety blockers, but the integration convention gaps are real silent-mispricing risks and the bench non-gate is a 'gate that does not gate'.

findings.location: crates/celnet-surface/src/lib.rs:69-89; sabr.rs:48,239 (SabrParams, SabrSmile, mod sabr); svi.rs:46 (SviSlice, mod svi); ssvi.rs:41,128 (SsviSurface, mod ssvi)
findings.issue: Public identifiers are named for mathematical methods/acronyms, not purpose. SABR (Stochastic-Alpha-Beta-Rho, Hagan et al.) and SVI/SSVI (Stochastic/Surface SVI, Gatheral & Jacquier) are method/paper names. Guardrail #8 forbids person/paper/framework/method names in public fn/type/trait/module/crate identifiers; provenance is doc-comment-only.
findings.why_it_matters: Hard rule violation. These are the surface crate's primary public API (re-exported at crate root), so every downstream consumer (engine, server, CLI, SDK) inherits the leaked method names into its own surface — this is exactly the vendor/method-neutral contract the guardrail protects, and it cannot be quietly refactored later under the no-versioned-API / one-clean-contract rule without churn across all callers.
findings.recommended_fix: Rename to purpose-named identifiers, e.g. SabrSmile->StochasticVolSmile, SabrParams->StochasticVolSmileParams, SviSlice->RawSmileSlice (or ParametricSmileSlice), SsviSurface->ParametricVolSurface, modules sabr/svi/ssvi->stochvol_smile/parametric_slice/parametric_surface. Move 'SABR'/'SVI'/'SSVI' provenance into the doc comments only.

findings.location: crates/celnet-gpu/src/philox.rs:81,122 (PhiloxAddress, PhiloxNormals, mod philox); lib.rs:42,47; crates/celnet-exotics/src/rng.rs:76 (PhiloxStream); celnet-gpu/src/cpu.rs:32 (rng: &PhiloxNormals)
findings.issue: 'Philox' is the proper name of the Salmon-Moraes-Dror-Shaw (SC'11) counter-based generator family used by Random123 — a framework/method name, not a purpose acronym. It is embedded in public type and module identifiers across two crates. The doc at philox.rs:17-20 even acknowledges the naming policy yet asserts the names are 'never person-named' — but the policy bars method/framework names too, not only person names.

findings.issue: mul_add (hardware FMA) is used in the streaming spot-perturbation path whose surrounding doc comments (tick.rs:36-39, stream.rs:158-159) explicitly advertise a 'deterministic perturbation discipline' shared bit-for-bit between the tick source and the RFS stream driver. The determinism guardrail says no FMA on reproducible paths; FMA fuses the multiply-add at a different rounding than separate mul+add and is not guaranteed bit-identical across targets/opt-levels.
findings.why_it_matters: If these perturbations are ever asserted bit-stable across platforms (the doc implies a shared 'discipline'), FMA can produce a 1-ulp divergence between two builds/architectures, breaking the claimed reproducibility. It is a simulation/demo feed rather than a priced reproducible path, so impact is limited — but the code claims determinism it cannot fully guarantee with mul_add.
findings.recommended_fix: Either replace the mul_add calls with explicit separate operations (u * 2.0 - 1.0 and base_spot * (u * BUMP + 1.0)) for true cross-target bit-stability, or soften the doc comments to state the determinism contract holds only within a single build/target and explicitly excludes FMA-fused rounding.

findings.location: crates/celnet-exotics/src/barrier.rs:182 (if rebate == 0.0); crates/celnet-surface/src/mathx.rs:22 (if x == 0.0); crates/celnet-integration/src/aggregate.rs:244 (if fw == 0.0); crates/celnet-surface/src/vannavolga.rs:225 (if forward == self.forward && t == self.t)
findings.issue: Direct float == comparisons on production paths, contrary to the blanket 'all float compare via is_close/assert_close, never ==' rule. Each is a defensible exact-sentinel/identity guard (zero-rebate short-circuit, x==0 limiting branch of powf, zero-weight skip, and an exact forward/time identity fast-path), but they are literal == on f64.
findings.why_it_matters: The guardrail is stated absolutely. The vannavolga.rs:225 case is the riskiest: it fast-paths only on an exact forward/time bit-match, so a forward/time that is numerically equal but differs by an ulp silently takes the slower rebuild branch — harmless to value but a latent inconsistency, and the pattern invites copy-paste of genuine == comparisons elsewhere.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a small allow-with-justification convention (e.g. an is_zero_sentinel helper or an explicit // float-eq: exact sentinel comment + clippy allow) for the true sentinel cases, and for vannavolga.rs:225 use is_close on forward and t (with a tight tol) rather than ==, so near-identical re-quotes hit the fast path.

It is fabricated/stale relative to the repo's own benchmark, contradicting the doc's stated verification posture and CLAUDE rule 'docs must match code (no stale or overstated claims)'. The real numbers (23-40 ns single, ~52 ns/option batched) are already excellent and beat the competitor field on their own merits — the fabrication is gratuitous self-harm.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace 8.85 ns / ~19 ns / 1.98 µs with the actual divan medians from benches/README.md (40.6 ns price, 23.4 ns price+Greeks, 3.33 µs / ~52 ns-per-option batch), or re-run cargo bench on the M4 and paste the verbatim output with the run date/host. Make the doc cite benches/README.md as the source so the two can never drift again. Keep the conservative per-option batched figure (~52 ns) as the headline since it is the cache-realistic one.

findings.issue: The matrix marks Asian and window breadth as '⛔ deferred', but both are actually implemented and non-trivial: crates/celnet-exotics/src/mc.rs:277 price_asian (Kemna-Vorst geometric control variate + antithetic, with closed-form geometric_asian_price at :363) and crates/celnet-exotics/src/lsv.rs:64/224/264 WindowBarrier (PDE + MC) plus adi.rs:312 WindowSpec. The doc UNDER-claims built capability while the latency rows OVER-claim.
findings.why_it_matters: In an adversarial competitive review, a doc that is simultaneously inflated (latency) and deflated (exotics breadth) signals the matrix was hand-maintained and is not actually synced to code, undermining the 'rows graduate only when test-backed' promise. Against SynOption/Fenics structured-product breadth, Celnet should be claiming the Asian + window-barrier coverage it actually has, not conceding it.
findings.recommended_fix: Split the deferred row: promote Asian (arithmetic+geometric, control-variate) and window-barrier to ✅ with the mc.rs/lsv.rs test references; keep only quanto + lookback (and the structured products) as ⛔. Verify each promoted row has a QuantLib/closed-form gated test before marking ✅.

findings.issue: The entire 'out-functions' thesis rests on a 'customer-extensible quant SDK (own models)' that SynOption/Fenics/Bloomberg all lack — but Celnet has only the API contract crate (celnet-plugin-api, 1167 LOC of types/WIT), NOT a working sandboxed host. The celnet-plugin-host crate does not exist; the doc itself marks it 🟡/⛔ (wasmtime deferred for RUSTSEC advisories).
findings.why_it_matters: The headline differentiator that supposedly beats every incumbent ('no competitor offers an open quant SDK') is currently undeliverable — a prospect cannot load a proprietary vol model or payoff. Until the host ships, the strongest 'out-functions' claim is aspirational, and a SynOption/Fenics evaluator will correctly score this a tie (neither side delivers customer models today).
findings.recommended_fix: Either (a) build celnet-plugin-host on a vetted wasm runtime (re-vet patched wasmtime, or use a pure-Rust interpreter like wasmi with fuel metering + deterministic replay) so the SDK is actually demonstrable, or (b) in every competitive comparison demote the SDK claim from 'out-functions today' to 'contract frozen, host on roadmap' and stop listing it as a current win. Pick one — do not keep it as a headline differentiator while it is unbuilt.

findings.issue: SynOption (Optimus), Fenics kACE and Bloomberg MARS all cover structured products — TARF, pivot TARF, accumulators/decumulators, KIKO — and Celnet has none of them (doc row 109 '⛔ deferred (scaffolded)'). For an FX-options e-trading desk, target-redemption forwards and accumulators are the highest-revenue structured flow; their absence is the biggest single functional gap vs the incumbent venues.
findings.why_it_matters: A 'beats SynOption' claim is not defensible while the competitor prices the structured products that drive real customer P&L and Celnet cannot. The LSV+MC+PDE engine substrate exists (lsv.rs, adi.rs, mc.rs), so this is a build-out, not an architecture gap — but until it lands, Celnet out-functions only on vanilla/first-gen-exotic surface, not on the structured book where SynOption monetizes.
findings.recommended_fix: Sequence TARF / accumulator / KIKO as the next exotics wave on the existing LSV+MC stack, each gated against QuantLib or published structured-product prices. Until shipped, the capability matrix must not imply parity — keep the ⛔ honest and add an explicit 'GAP vs SynOption/Fenics' callout in the executive summary rather than burying it in row 109.

findings.location: docs/CAPABILITIES-VS-COMPETITION.md (no asset-class breadth row) ; crates/celnet-types/src/lib.rs, crates/celnet-conventions/src/lib.rs:200
findings.issue: SynOption explicitly covers 75 currency pairs and is moving into crypto options (Synchro / OrBit Markets partnership, per COMPETITIVE-ANALYSIS.md:27). Celnet's conventions/calendar layer is built for ~8-9 G10 pairs + a couple of EM NDFs (USDKRW), with 8 currency calendars; there is no crypto-options or precious-metals (XAU/XAG) coverage, and no documented path to the breadth SynOption advertises.
findings.why_it_matters: Breadth of tradeable pairs/asset classes is a first-order procurement criterion. A desk evaluating Celnet vs Optimus will see ~9 pairs vs 75 and crypto-options absent vs SynOption's Synchro. The convention/calendar correctness edge is real and valuable, but it is demonstrated on a narrow universe; the 'out-intuits on convention transparency' claim is strongest precisely where it is hardest to scale (EM/exotic-ccy conventions are where ambiguity actually bites).
findings.recommended_fix: Add an explicit asset-class/pair-coverage row to the matrix stating the honest current count vs SynOption's 75. Prioritize widening the convention+calendar tables to the full G10+EM set (and decide crypto-options in/out of scope explicitly). Frame the convention-transparency edge as 'correct on the pairs we cover' rather than implying universal coverage.

findings.location: docs/CAPABILITIES-VS-COMPETITION.md:118 ('Multi-source surface aggregation + divergence ✅ ... counters Primus') ; crates/celnet-integration/src/aggregate.rs, divergence.rs
findings.issue: The doc claims the integration aggregation '✅ counters Primus's core feature'. The code (aggregate.rs staleness_weight, divergence.rs SourceDivergence/divergence_report) is a genuine time-weighted-staleness + divergence-detection engine — credible — but Primus's value is breadth of ingested bank/broker feeds + the curated fair-mid across 75 pairs, not just the math. Celnet has the algorithm but no actual multi-bank feed inventory or coverage proof.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Counters Primus' overstates parity: matching the aggregation algorithm is necessary but not sufficient against a vendor whose moat is the LP/broker feed panel and pair coverage. An evaluator will ask 'which feeds, how many sources, which pairs' — and the answer is the FMD-style normalizer plus test fixtures, not a live multi-bank panel.
findings.recommended_fix: Soften the claim to '✅ aggregation+divergence math (algorithmic parity); feed-panel breadth is integration-wave work' and back it with the actual number of distinct source adapters wired. Treat the LP/broker feed inventory as a named gap, since that — not the time-decay formula — is what makes Primus sticky.

findings.issue: The matrix lists 'Customer quant SDK 🟡', 'click-to-trade 🟡 v2', and treats execution as future, but the wire contract AND server already implement the full RFQ→Quote→Accept→Execution lifecycle with idempotent booking and last-look validity (crates/celnet-server/src/services/quote.rs:258-323, celnet-proto QuoteAccept/QuoteReject/Execution). The single-dealer click-to-trade/booking path is built, not deferred.
findings.why_it_matters: Under-claiming a real, tested execution-booking lifecycle weakens the RFQ comparison vs SynOption/Murex where 'RFQ lifecycle ✅' is conceded to competitors. Celnet should claim its idempotent accept→execution booking explicitly; what is genuinely a non-goal is the regulated MULTI-bank venue (correctly marked ✱), not single-dealer execution.
findings.recommended_fix: Promote 'single-dealer click-to-trade / quote-accept→execution booking' to ✅ with the quote.rs reference, and keep only the multi-bank RMO venue as ✱ non-goal. Distinguish 'execution booking' (built) from 'regulated venue' (non-goal) so the row reads accurately.

findings.location: docs/CAPABILITIES-VS-COMPETITION.md:3,144 ('435 tests') vs repo (~447 test occurrences)
findings.issue: The doc pins '435 tests green' as a headline verification figure; a rough grep of test attributes across src+tests yields ~447 occurrences (proptest/tokio::test inflate this, so the true nextest count may differ either way). The exact number is asserted but not pinned to a reproducible command output.
findings.why_it_matters: A precise count stated as proof must be reproducible on demand; if an evaluator runs nextest and gets a different number, it erodes the 'every claim test-backed' posture even when the suite is genuinely strong.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace the hard-coded '435' with the verbatim tail of `cargo nextest run` (test count + pass line) captured at a stated date, or stop quoting an exact integer and say 'full suite green via just check'. Keep it self-verifying.

findings.issue: Celnet correctly identifies FIX connectivity (designed only, row 123 🟡) and front-end GUI (✱ via Celer) as gaps, but SynOption/Fenics/Bloomberg all ship FIX STP and a trader GUI today. Without FIX, Celnet cannot STP into the bank risk systems that every incumbent integrates with, and without a GUI a desk cannot adopt it standalone.
findings.why_it_matters: These are table-stakes for desk adoption, not differentiators. The gRPC/WS typed contract is genuinely better than BLPAPI/FIX for programmatic MMs, but a desk still needs FIX to book into its existing estate and a screen for human traders. 'Beats SynOption' is not defensible for the human-trader and STP segments until FIX + a UI exist (even via Celer).
findings.recommended_fix: Keep FIX and GUI as explicit named gaps in the executive summary (not just buried rows). Commit to a FIX destination adapter in the integration wave and confirm the Celer front end actually renders Celnet's surface/RFQ, so the 'GUI via Celer' claim is demonstrable rather than assumed.

overall: Celnet is a genuinely strong, high-quality codebase (~33k LOC, ~447 test occurrences, real SSVI/SABR arb-free surfaces, real Kemna-Vorst Asian + window-barrier exotics, real LSV particle calibration at 1009 LOC, real wgpu+WGSL GPU path with f64 CPU oracle, a fully-wired idempotent RFQ→Execution lifecycle, and solid determinism discipline — no FMA on numeric paths, timeout-bounded async tests, no schema_version, libm-routed math). On the audit lane specifically: the COMPETITIVE-ANALYSIS.md competitor breakdown is accurate and well-researched, and Celnet does plausibly out-INTUIT the field on convention transparency and auditable arbitrage-free surfaces, and out-PERFORM on real (re-measured) latency. BUT the 'beats SynOption' thesis has one BLOCKER and several real GAPS. The blocker: the headline latency numbers in CAPABILITIES-VS-COMPETITION.md (8.85 ns / ~19 ns / 1.98 µs) are fabricated — they contradict the repo's own bench README (40.6 / 23.4 / 3.33) and appear nowhere in code, fatally undermining the 'no claim not in the code' posture on the very 'out-performs' cell that distinguishes Celnet from every competitor. The gaps that block a defensible state-of-the-art claim: (1) the customer-extensible quant SDK — the centerpiece 'out-functions' differentiator no incumbent has — is only an API contract, with no working host; (2) no structured products (TARF/accumulator/pivot) where SynOption/Fenics monetize; (3) ~9 pairs vs SynOption's 75 and no crypto/metals; (4) FIX STP and a trader GUI are table-stakes that are designed-only/non-goal. The doc also simultaneously under-claims built capability (Asian, window barriers, execution booking) and over-claims aggregation parity with Primus. Net: Celnet out-performs and out-intuits on a narrow, deep G10-vanilla/first-gen-exotic core, but does not yet out-function SynOption on structured-product breadth, pair/asset coverage, multi-bank liquidity, or a deliverable extensibility SDK. Fix the fabricated numbers first (credibility), then close the SDK-host and structured-product gaps to make the 'beats SynOption' claim defensible.
